links.title: Poltava Museum of Long-Range and Strategic Aviation

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The 300th anniversary of the Battle of Poltava in 2009 highlighted competing Ukrainian and Russian memories of Mazepa. The oblast supported the Orange Revolution and Euromaidan.

crimea-donbas-war.summary: The oblast sent volunteers and units to the Donbas and hosted displaced people. Poltava's KrAZ produced military trucks for the army.
crimea-donbas-war.military: The Myrhorod-based 831st Tactical Aviation Brigade flew in the Donbas war.

full-scale-invasion.summary: Russian forces did not reach the oblast, but on 27 June 2022 a Kh-22 missile destroyed the Amstor shopping mall in Kremenchuk, killing over 20 people. The Kremenchuk refinery was repeatedly struck and put out of action.
full-scale-invasion.military: Myrhorod air base was a frequent target; the oblast became a logistics hub for the eastern front.

war-of-attrition.summary: On 3 September 2024 two ballistic missiles hit the Military Institute of Communications in Poltava, killing about 60 people in one of the deadliest single strikes of the war. Kremenchuk's industry and gas facilities were also hit.
war-of-attrition.military: The Poltava strike killed many cadets and servicemen; drones targeted Myrhorod air base.

war-2025-2026.summary: Russian drones and missiles repeatedly struck gas production and processing sites in the oblast, Ukraine's main gas-producing region, and the Kremenchuk refinery in 2025-2026, cutting output and causing local power and heating outages.
war-2025-2026.military: No ground fighting; air defence protected Poltava, Kremenchuk and the energy infrastructure.

UA-35.name: Kirovohrad Oblast
UA-35.overview: Kirovohrad Oblast lies in the centre of Ukraine between the Dnieper and the Southern Bug, where the forest-steppe gives way to the steppe. Its land held the Trypillia mega-site of Nebelivka, the namesake sites of the Bronze Age Sabatynivka culture and the rich Scythian Melgunov kurgan, then for most of the medieval period lay in the nomad steppe of Pechenegs, Cumans and the Golden Horde, and later in the Wild Fields at the edge of the Zaporozhian lands. Russia colonised it from the 1750s with New Serbia and the Fortress of St Elizabeth, the origin of today's Kropyvnytskyi, where the Ukrainian professional theatre was born in 1882. The region suffered the civil war, the Holodomor and Nazi occupation, and since 2022 has been a rear region targeted by missile and drone strikes.

trypillia.summary: The Nebelivka mega-site near Novoarkhanhelsk, covering about 238 hectares around 4000 BCE, is one of the largest Trypillia settlements, with a huge central 'mega-structure' excavated in 2009-2014. Trypillia villages filled the western part of the oblast.

bronze-age-steppe.summary: The Late Bronze Age Sabatynivka culture is named after the village of Sabatynivka on the Southern Bug in the oblast; its farmers and herders built settlements with stone houses and bronze-casting workshops. Earlier Yamnaya and Catacomb kurgans are widespread.

cimmerians.control: Cimmerian-era nomads (Belozerka culture) and Chornyi Lis farmers
cimmerians.summary: The southern steppe districts lay in the Cimmerian world, while the northern forest-steppe near the Tiasmyn and Inhul belonged to the Chornyi Lis culture.

scythians.summary: In 1763 the Melgunov (Lytoi) kurgan near Yelisavetgrad yielded a 7th-6th century BCE Scythian royal burial with a gold sword sheath of Near Eastern style, the first scientifically recorded Scythian find. The north of the oblast was part of the forest-steppe Tiasmyn group.
scythians.military: Scythian warrior kurgans with weapons and horse harness are common in the steppe districts.

sarmatians.summary: Sarmatian nomads replaced the Scythians in the steppe and pastured herds along the Inhul and Inhulets, leaving kurgan burials.

goths-chernyakhov.summary: Chernyakhov villages spread into the forest-steppe north and along the river valleys of the steppe, with Roman imports. The area was part of the Greuthungi-Gothic domain.

huns.summary: The Hunnic invasion of the 370s destroyed the Chernyakhov settlements, and the steppe became Hunnic pasture.

antes.summary: Slavic Penkovka culture villages, associated with the Antes, occupied the northern river valleys, while Bulgar and Avar nomads moved through the steppe.

east-slavic-tribes.control: Khazar sphere; Magyar pastures (Etelköz); Ulichians in the north-west
east-slavic-tribes.summary: In the 9th century the Magyars grazed their herds in the land of Etelköz between the Dnieper and Danube, which included this region, before moving to Pannonia around 895. Ulichian Slavs held the north-western forest-steppe.

kyivan-rus-formation.summary: The Pechenegs drove out the Magyars around 895 and dominated the region's steppe, threatening Rus' trade on the Dnieper.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: The region remained Pecheneg steppe beyond Volodymyr's defensive lines on the Ros and Sula; Byzantine sources describe Pecheneg clans in this area.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: After Yaroslav's victory of 1036 the Pechenegs weakened, and Turkic Torks and then Cumans moved into the steppe.

rus-fragmentation.summary: The region formed part of Cumania; stone 'babas' (kurgan stelae) of the Cumans have been found in its steppe districts.
rus-fragmentation.military: Rus' princes' campaigns against the Cumans occasionally crossed the steppe toward the Dnieper rapids.

galicia-volhynia.summary: The steppe stayed in Cuman hands, nominally beyond any Rus' principality.

mongol-period.summary: After 1240 the region became Horde pastureland. Around 1362 Lithuania's Algirdas defeated three Tatar beys at Blue Waters, probably on the Syniukha River on the oblast's western edge, though the exact site is disputed.
mongol-period.military: The Battle of Blue Waters (c. 1362) broke Horde control of the lands west of the Dnieper.

lithuania-poland.control: Nominally Lithuanian; Wild Fields frontier with the Crimean Khanate
lithuania-poland.summary: The region formed part of the 'Wild Fields', an almost empty steppe crossed by Crimean Tatar raiding routes such as the Black Trail. Ukrainian 'ukhodnyky' came seasonally to fish, hunt and keep bees.
lithuania-poland.military: Tatar raids followed the Black Trail across the region toward Podolia and Volhynia.

commonwealth.control: Wild Fields between the Commonwealth, Zaporozhian Cossacks and Crimea
commonwealth.summary: Polish claims reached the Tiasmyn, but the steppe was used by Zaporozhian Cossacks and Tatars. Cossack winter settlements (zymivnyky) appeared along the Inhul and Inhulets.
commonwealth.military: Cossack patrols and Tatar raiders clashed in the steppe.

cossack-hetmanate.control: Zaporozhian Host lands and Chyhyryn regiment's southern fringe
cossack-hetmanate.summary: The northern districts belonged to the Chyhyryn and Kropyvna regimental lands of the Hetmanate, while the steppe was Zaporozhian territory. Settlement remained sparse.
cossack-hetmanate.military: Tatar allies of Khmelnytsky and Polish forces passed through the region.

the-ruin.summary: The wars of the Ruin and Ottoman campaigns left the region nearly empty. Under the 1681 Treaty of Bakhchisarai, the land between the Southern Bug and Dnieper was to remain unsettled.

hetmanate-decline.control: Russian Empire (New Serbia); Zaporozhian Liberties in the south-east
hetmanate-decline.summary: In 1752 Russia created New Serbia, a military colony of Serbian, Vlach and other Balkan settlers on Zaporozhian land, with its centre at Novomyrhorod. The Fortress of St Elizabeth, built in 1754, grew into the town of Yelisavetgrad, today's Kropyvnytskyi.
hetmanate-decline.military: The Fortress of St Elizabeth anchored Russian defences against the Crimean Khanate; the Crimean Khan Qırım Giray besieged the region in 1769 in the last great Tatar raid.

partitions-crimea.control: Russian Empire (New Russia, then Yekaterinoslav Viceroyalty)
partitions-crimea.summary: After the destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich in 1775 and the annexation of Crimea in 1783, the region ceased to be a frontier and was rapidly colonised by Ukrainian, Russian and foreign settlers. The western districts across the Syniukha joined Russia with the Second Partition of Poland in 1793.

two-empires.summary: The area belonged to Yelisavetgrad uyezd of Kherson Governorate, with large estates and military settlements of the imperial cavalry. Yelisavetgrad grew as a grain trading and fair town.
two-empires.military: Military settlements of cavalry regiments were established around Yelisavetgrad from 1817, and the town later hosted a cavalry cadet school.

national-revival.summary: In 1882 Marko Kropyvnytsky founded the first professional Ukrainian theatre troupe in Yelisavetgrad, with Ivan Karpenko-Karyi, Mykola Sadovsky and Panas Saksahansky. The town was also the starting point of the 1881 wave of anti-Jewish pogroms, and Leon Trotsky was born in 1879 at a farm near Bereslavka.

ukrainian-revolution.control: Ukrainian People's Republic, then the Hetmanate
ukrainian-revolution.summary: The region came under the UNR and then the Hetmanate with Austro-Hungarian and German troops. Former tsarist officer Nykyfor Hryhoriv from the Oleksandriia area raised peasant forces against the occupiers in late 1918.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Hryhoriv's insurgents fought German and Austro-Hungarian troops and joined the Directory's uprising.

soviet-takeover.control: Bolsheviks, Hryhoriv's insurgents, Whites; Soviet by 1920
soviet-takeover.summary: In May 1919 Hryhoriv turned against the Bolsheviks, and his men carried out a pogrom in Yelisavetgrad; he was killed by Makhno's men in July 1919. The region passed between Reds, Whites and insurgents before Soviet control in 1920.
soviet-takeover.military: Hryhoriv's uprising (May 1919) was based in the region; Makhno's Insurgent Army operated nearby.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Yelisavetgrad was renamed Zinovievsk in 1924 and became an agricultural machinery centre (Chervona Zirka plant). NEP restored the grain economy.

holodomor-terror.control: Ukrainian SSR (Odesa and Mykolaiv oblasts; Kirovohrad Oblast from 1939)
holodomor-terror.summary: The region's grain villages suffered heavily in the Holodomor. The city was renamed Kirovo in 1934 and Kirovohrad in 1939, when Kirovohrad Oblast was created.

soviet-annexations.summary: The new oblast developed agricultural machine-building in Kirovohrad and brown-coal mining around Oleksandriia.

nazi-occupation.control: German occupation (Reichskommissariat Ukraine), Aug 1941 to Jan-Mar 1944
nazi-occupation.summary: German forces occupied the region in August 1941 and murdered its Jews; a large POW camp operated in Kirovohrad. The Holocaust and forced labour deportations depleted the population.
nazi-occupation.military: The Soviet Kirovograd offensive liberated the city on 8 January 1944, and the rest of the oblast was freed by March 1944.

postwar-ussr.summary: The towns were rebuilt and the Chervona Zirka plant resumed production of seeders. The 1946-47 famine affected the grain districts.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: The Kremenchuk hydroelectric dam and the new town of Svitlovodsk were built on the oblast's Dnieper edge around 1960. Uranium ore mining developed in the Novokostiantynivka and Mykhailivka areas.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Kanatove air base near Kirovohrad served Soviet military aviation.

independence.summary: The oblast remained agrarian, with uranium mining important for Ukraine's nuclear power. Population declined in rural districts.
independence.military: Kanatove became a base of the Ukrainian Air Force's flight training.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The oblast largely supported Yushchenko in 2004; Euromaidan protesters rallied in Kirovohrad in 2013-14.

crimea-donbas-war.summary: Under the 2015 decommunisation laws Kirovohrad was renamed Kropyvnytskyi in 2016, after the theatre founder Marko Kropyvnytsky; the oblast's name stayed unchanged pending a constitutional amendment. The region sent troops to the Donbas.
crimea-donbas-war.military: The 3rd Special Purpose Regiment, based in Kropyvnytskyi, fought at Donetsk Airport in 2014-15.

full-scale-invasion.summary: Russian forces did not reach the oblast, but missile strikes hit Kanatove air base and infrastructure in Kropyvnytskyi and Oleksandriia from the first day. The region received large numbers of displaced people from the south and east.
full-scale-invasion.military: Strikes targeted the air base, rail hubs and fuel depots.

war-of-attrition.summary: The oblast was a rear logistics area for the southern front, periodically hit by drones and missiles aimed at airfields, energy and rail facilities.

war-2025-2026.summary: Drone attacks on Kropyvnytskyi, Oleksandriia and energy infrastructure continued in 2025-2026, causing outages; the oblast stayed far from the ground front, which in parts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast moved somewhat closer during 2025.
war-2025-2026.military: No ground fighting; air defence and mobile groups countered Shahed drones.
